prompt: How does the material define "reasoning"?

options.text: Engaging in logical, rational and analytical thinking
Memorizing scripture passages verbatim
Performing physical labor to demonstrate faith
Relying solely on emotional intuition

explanation: 'To reason implies to engage in rational, logical and analytical thinking. It also means good judgment; sound sense.' Three adjectives, and the second definition adds judgment and sound sense.

why.a: Correct. Logical, rational and analytical are the three words used, in the book's own definition.
why.b: Wrong. The author explicitly rejects cramming: asked whether he crams scriptures he said no, he eats them.
why.c: Wrong. Physical labour is never equated with reasoning; the book says to sit down and think BEFORE running around.
why.d: Wrong. Emotional intuition is the opposite of analytical thinking, and the prodigal son is praised for reasoning rather than feeling.

prompt: What does the passage give as the end product of reasoning?

options.text: Quality decisions
Settled convictions
Clear communication
Peace of mind

explanation: 'And what is the end product? Quality decisions. Reasoning enhances the quality of decisions you make.' It is asked and answered in one breath.

why.a: Correct. Quality decisions, stated as the end product and then repeated.
why.b: Wrong. Conviction is used in Chapter 1 to define belief, not as reasoning's output.
why.c: Wrong. Communication is never discussed as a product of reasoning.
why.d: Wrong. Peace is a product of divine WISDOM in Chapter 5, which makes it a fair guess in the wrong chapter.

prompt: Which scripture contains God's invitation "Come now, and let us reason together"?

options.text: Isaiah 1:18
Isaiah 41:21
Isaiah 43:18
Isaiah 55:8

explanation: Isaiah 1:18, and its verse 19 is quoted right after: 'If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land.' The book uses several Isaiah citations, so keeping them apart matters.

why.a: Correct. Isaiah 1:18 is the reason together verse.
why.b: Wrong. Isaiah 41:21 is 'Produce your cause... bring forth your strong reasons', quoted a few lines later in the same section.
why.c: Wrong. Isaiah 43:18 is 'Remember ye not the former things', from Chapter 9 on the trap of past failures.
why.d: Wrong. Isaiah 55:8 is God's ways being higher than your ways, from Chapter 6.

topic: eat the good of the land
prompt: According to verse 19, what condition must one meet to "eat the good of the land"?

options.text: Be willing and obedient
Be highly educated
Be wealthy and powerful
Be physically strong

explanation: Isaiah 1:19: 'If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land.' The author draws from it that reasoning is required to gain access into your inheritance on earth.

why.a: Correct. Willing and obedient are the two conditions in the verse.
why.b: Wrong. Education is repeatedly demoted in this book, which says no school has a Faculty of Success.
why.c: Wrong. Wealth is a product of wisdom, never a precondition of blessing here.
why.d: Wrong. Physical strength is never a condition anywhere in the book.

prompt: What method did the individual mentioned in the passage use to return to colour and beauty?

options.text: He reasoned his way back
He prayed
He fasted
He performed miracles

explanation: The prodigal son. 'There's nowhere we were told that he prayed or fasted. All he did was to reason his way back to colour and beauty.' The denial of prayer and fasting is explicit, which is what makes those the trap options.

why.a: Correct. He came to himself, reasoned, and returned; the book calls it reasoning his way back to a colourful destiny.
why.b: Wrong, and it is deliberately baited. The passage names prayer only to say there is nowhere we are told he prayed.
why.c: Wrong, for the same reason. Fasting is named in the same denial.
why.d: Wrong. No miracle appears in the parable or in the book's use of it.

prompt: What questions does the passage imagine the prodigal son asking himself?

options.text: Where am I? How did I get here? Do I want to be out of here? What does it take to get where I'm going?
Who has wronged me, and how shall I answer them?
What have I done, and can I ever be forgiven?
Who will go with me, and who will stay behind?

explanation: The four questions are diagnostic and forward looking, which is the model of reasoning the book wants: locate your position, trace the cause, decide the destination, then cost the route.

why.a: Correct. These four questions are given in this order, and they mirror the tower builder counting the cost.
why.b: Wrong. Blame plays no part; the parable's man blames himself and then moves.
why.c: Wrong. Guilt appears in his speech to his father, but the questions the book imagines are practical rather than penitential.
why.d: Wrong. Companions are never part of this illustration.

topic: God will not think for you
prompt: What does the passage say about God and your thinking?

options.text: No matter how hard you pray, God will not think for you; it is your responsibility to think
God thinks through you when you yield to Him
God will supply the thought if you supply the willingness
God prefers that you act first and think afterwards

explanation: 'God won't think or plan the food you'll eat for you. No matter how hard you pray, God won't think for you. It's your responsibility to think, not His.' It follows the charge that the Church has long lost the art of thinking.

why.a: Correct. The responsibility is placed on you, explicitly and against the appeal to prayer.
why.b: Wrong. This is close to the inspiration doctrine of Chapter 6, but even there the Spirit moves in YOUR mental faculty rather than replacing your thinking.
why.c: Wrong. Willingness is the condition for eating the good of the land, not a trade in which God does the thinking.
why.d: Wrong. The book's order is always to sit down and think first.

prompt: According to the parable cited in Luke 14:28, what should a person do before beginning to build a tower?

options.text: Sit down and count the cost
Start building immediately without planning
Ask friends for financial help
Pray and hope for success

explanation: 'For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?' The author's line on it: every tower builder is a tower thinker.

why.a: Correct. Sitting down first and counting the cost is the parable's own instruction.
why.b: Wrong. This is exactly the running here and there Chapter 1 tells you to stop.
why.c: Wrong. Borrowing is condemned in Chapter 5, where the author resolves never to need to borrow.
why.d: Wrong. Hoping without counting is what the parable warns against, and the book keeps ranking thinking above unaccompanied prayer.

topic: Jesus and the woman caught in adultery
prompt: How does the passage interpret Jesus writing on the ground when the woman caught in adultery was brought to Him?

options.text: He was engaged in the art of reasoning, thinking the issue through as if He had not heard them
He was writing out the sins of her accusers
He was showing that the law was written by God's finger
He was waiting for the crowd to grow quiet

explanation: The book reads it as a demonstration of reasoning: He stooped down, wrote as if He had not heard them, thought the issue through, and then looked up with John 8:7, 'He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.'

why.a: Correct. Reasoning is the explicit interpretation offered, and it is why the episode appears in this section.
why.b: Wrong. Listing their sins is a common traditional guess that this book does not make.
why.c: Wrong. The finger of God is another traditional reading, absent here.
why.d: Wrong. Waiting for quiet is not the reason given; the thinking is.

prompt: What does the passage say reasoning guarantees?

options.text: A rising
A reward
A rest
A refuge

explanation: 'What does reasoning guarantee? It guarantees a rising.' The word is chosen against the prodigal son's own 'I will arise and go to my father', and it makes reasoning a high-flier in the race of life.

why.a: Correct. A rising, which links back to the prodigal son arising and going to his father.
why.b: Wrong. Reward language is not used of reasoning.
why.c: Wrong. Rest on every side is what God gave Solomon through wisdom in Chapter 5, a different chapter and a different cause.
why.d: Wrong. Refuge never appears in this book.

prompt: How long did the author say it took of sitting down and planning before the ministry was commissioned?

options.text: 26 months
20 years
3 days
40 years

explanation: 26 months of first sitting down and planning, through mental processing of objectives. The 20 years in the same passage is something else: the STRUCTURE they would use for the next 20 years was already in place.

why.a: Correct. Twenty-six months of planning before the doors opened.
why.b: Wrong. Twenty years is how far ahead the structure was designed to serve, not how long the planning took.
why.c: Wrong. The 3-day trip is the prosperity study in Chapter 7.
why.d: Wrong. About forty years is David Yonggi Cho's time in ministry in Chapter 8.

prompt: What detail does the passage give about how the ministry began?

options.text: It was commissioned on a Saturday, work started in the office the following Monday, and it has remained open ever since
It began in a rented hall with fifteen people
It began only after a long period of fasting
It opened without any plan, and the plan followed later

explanation: The days matter to the point being made, which is readiness: everything they would need was already in place before they started, so there was no gap between commissioning and operation.

why.a: Correct. Saturday to Monday, and open ever since, which is offered as proof of what planning buys.
why.b: Wrong. The gathering of about fifteen people is the all-night meeting story in Chapter 11.
why.c: Wrong. Fasting is not credited anywhere in this book with producing results.
why.d: Wrong. This inverts the entire point of the anecdote.

prompt: What conclusion does the author draw from the man whose income rose from one thousand to twenty thousand naira and was always enough?

options.text: That what you have is enough, if only you can think well
That contentment is the secret of a happy life
That income always rises to meet a person's needs
That God multiplies whatever is given to Him

explanation: 'This goes to confirm my belief that what you have is enough, if only you can think well.' Repeated a line later as: if you can think enough, what you have is enough.

why.a: Correct. Thinking, not income, is the variable the story isolates.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the closest trap. Contentment sounds like the moral but the book's word is THINK; it is a claim about mental capacity, not about lowered expectation.
why.c: Wrong. The passage gives a counter example of people earning fifty thousand who have built nothing.
why.d: Wrong. Giving is not part of this anecdote.

prompt: How does the passage explain why a person borrows?

options.text: You are borrowing because you can't think enough, not because you don't have enough
You are borrowing because you have not given enough
You are borrowing because you were not taught to save
You are borrowing because the economy leaves you no choice

explanation: 'You're not a beggar because you don't have enough, you're borrowing because you can't think enough.' The author adds that when he earned three hundred naira he did not borrow and always had brought forward.

why.a: Correct. Thinking, not resources, is named as the cause, in the book's characteristic reversal.
why.b: Wrong. Giving belongs to the prosperity discussion in Chapter 4, not to this diagnosis.
why.c: Wrong. Saving habits are never discussed.
why.d: Wrong. Chapter 2 explicitly tells you to stop thinking lack because of your country's economy, since you are not your country's economist.

topic: the old parents who built houses
prompt: What does the passage say about how our old parents built houses?

options.text: Most were peasant farmers, some never even saw one hundred naira together at a time, but they still built houses
They built slowly over several generations
They built with communal labour rather than money
They built because land was free in their day

explanation: The contrast is with people earning fifty thousand naira a month who have not built a room, a case of the more the income, the greater the waste.

why.a: Correct. Peasant farmers, never one hundred naira together at a time, and yet houses were built.
why.b: Wrong. Generations are not mentioned; the point is that individuals did it on almost nothing.
why.c: Wrong. Communal labour is a plausible historical explanation that the book does not give.
why.d: Wrong. Land costs are never raised, and offering an external excuse would undercut the argument that thinking is the variable.

prompt: Which statement does the passage make about what is seen and what is unseen?

options.text: Everything you see on the outside begins from the inside, and everything you see in the open started in the secret
What is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal
What is hidden will always be brought to light
The outside is a poor guide to what is within

explanation: The pairing is inside then outside, secret then open, and it grounds the whole insistence on sitting down to think before acting.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are in the sentence, and both run from hidden cause to visible effect.
why.b: Wrong. That is a genuine Pauline sentence from elsewhere that this book does not quote.
why.c: Wrong. The nearest thing in the book is Job 28 on the thing that is hid being brought forth to light, which is about wisdom rather than about this claim.
why.d: Wrong. The book relies on visible results as evidence, so it would not say this.

prompt: Which scripture is quoted as "Produce your cause... bring forth your strong reasons"?

options.text: Isaiah 41:21
Isaiah 1:18
Jeremiah 33:3
Job 32:8

explanation: Isaiah 41:21, cited to show that God expects you to be a deep thinker so you can bring forth strong reasons.

why.a: Correct. Isaiah 41:21 is the strong reasons verse.
why.b: Wrong. Isaiah 1:18 is the reason together invitation from a few lines earlier in the same section.
why.c: Wrong. Jeremiah 33:3 is 'Call unto me, and I will answer thee', used in Chapter 8 for insight-expectant prayer.
why.d: Wrong. Job 32:8 is the inspiration verse that anchors Chapter 6.

prompt: Fill the blank: "Every tower builder is a tower {{1}}."
explanation: Thinker. Planner is close in sense and is the trap, but the book's line turns on thinking, which is its master word throughout.

prompt: The passage states that the prodigal son fasted and prayed before deciding to return to his father.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False, and emphatically so: 'There's nowhere we were told that he prayed or fasted. All he did was to reason his way back.' The absence of prayer and fasting is the whole point of choosing this example.

why.true: Wrong. This is the religiously expected answer, which is exactly why the book denies it so plainly.
why.false: Correct. He reasoned; there is no record of prayer or fasting, and the passage says so directly.

topic: the more the income the greater the waste
prompt: What phrase does the passage use for people whose spending grows with their earnings?

options.text: The more the income, the greater the waste
A rising tide that lifts nothing
Rich in hand, poor in habit
Earning much and keeping little

explanation: 'For them, it's a case of the more the income, the greater the waste.' It describes people earning fifty thousand naira a month who have not built even a room.

why.a: Correct. This is the phrase as printed.
why.b: Wrong. A plausible aphorism that does not appear in the book.
why.c: Wrong. Another invented saying in the right register but not in the text.
why.d: Wrong. It captures the sense but not the words, and these questions turn on the exact wording.
